nameStory: Cambridge Milk-parsley earned its name because in England, it's found only in the county of Cambridgeshire, making it incredibly rare there. The 'milk-parsley' part comes from its close resemblance to another wetland plant called milk parsley, though they're actually different species. It's like having a botanical doppelganger that shares the same neighborhood!
description: Cambridge Milk-parsley is a delicate member of the carrot family that loves wet feet and grows in marshes and damp meadows. This slender plant produces the classic umbrella-shaped white flower clusters typical of its family, sitting atop solid green stems. Its leaves are finely divided and feathery, resembling those of caraway (hence its scientific name carvifolia, meaning 'caraway-leaved'). It's quite rare in New England, with only a handful of known locations.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Solid, greenish stems that feel firm when gently squeezed - never hollow or purplish like some similar species

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Finely divided, feathery leaves with sharp-pointed leaflets that are darker green than similar plants - the tips feel distinctly pointed to the touch

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers arranged in flat-topped umbrella clusters (umbels) with small bracts that stand upright rather than drooping down

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: When in fruit, look for three raised ridges (wings) running along the back of each seed - these feel slightly raised when rubbed gently

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows 2-4 feet tall in clumps, preferring to keep its feet wet in marshy conditions rather than dry upland areas

habitat: Cambridge Milk-parsley is a wetland specialist that thrives in fens, wet meadows, and marshy areas with consistently moist or saturated soils. In New England, look for it in calcareous (lime-rich) wetlands and along the edges of slow-moving streams or seasonal flood plains. It prefers areas that stay wet through most of the growing season but aren't permanently flooded.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the weather warms, with the characteristic feathery foliage unfurling from the wet soil. Young leaves are the best time to examine the sharp-pointed leaflet tips.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with white umbrella-shaped flower clusters appearing from mid to late summer. This is the easiest time for identification when flowers are fresh.
seasonality.fall: Fruits develop and mature, showing the distinctive winged ridges that help separate it from similar species. Leaves begin to yellow and die back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground parts, leaving no above-ground traces. The wet habitat may be marked by dried stems of other wetland plants.

funFact: This plant is so rare in England that it grows in only three small Cambridgeshire fens, making it one of the country's most endangered members of the carrot family - yet here in New England, it's naturalized and managing to make itself at home in our wetlands!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Milk Parsley, but Cambridge Milk-parsley has solid green stems (not hollow and purplish), sharp-pointed dark green leaflets (not blunt and pale), and upright bracts under the flowers (not drooping). Memory trick: 'Cambridge Correct' - solid stems standing correctly upright, sharp leaflets pointing correctly up.
contextualKnowledge: In its native Europe, this species is called simply 'Milk Parsley' in many regions, but in North America it's sometimes known as 'Little-leaf Angelica,' which can be confusing since it's not a true angelica. The common names reflect its resemblance to other carrot family members rather than close relationships.
compareHints: Cambridge Milk-parsley is the only Selinum species found in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Compared to other carrot family wetland species like Water Hemlock or Angelica, it's more delicate overall with finer, more divided leaves and smaller flower clusters. Its solid stems and sharp leaflet tips are key features that set it apart from most other white-flowered wetland umbellifers in our region.
